subject: lion
pitch: A proud old lion resting with his head held high. A huge shaggy mane fading from golden blond at the face to dark chocolate at the edges, a tawny body with a pale cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, a broad black nose, a scar across one eyebrow, big padded paws and a long tail ending in a dark tuft.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the proportions of a lion model, estimating realistic heights for hips, shoulders, and head, before planning out the skeleton joints in a TypeScript module using the SDK.

Building spine and neck chains...

Checking the knee bend direction and leg reach for the front limb — the shoulder-to-paw distance needs to match the segment lengths, so I'm adjusting shoulder height and limb lengths until the target foot position is actually reachable.

For the paws I'll keep things simple with padded sphere-like shapes rather than individual toes, using the scale option on the part geometry to shape them appropriately.

Now I'm working out the hind legs with a three-segment chain—hip, knee, and hock down to the foot—positioning the hip joint up and back and the foot target forward and low, so the bend pattern reads naturally like a lion's hind leg.

I'm also planning the tail as a separate joint chain curving backward and down from the hips toward the ground, and sketching the body as a sweep along the spine with a varying radius profile to give the chest more bulk than the hindquarters.

For color, I'm using sectors around the sweep to create countershading—tawny on top and cream along the belly. For the mane, I'm weighing options between a ring of tubes along the neck or card geometry with a generated fur-tuft texture to get a shaggy look.

For the mane texture, I'm sketching a single tapering tuft SVG applied to cards, then tinting each card with a gradient paint that shifts from golden blond near the face to dark chocolate toward the outer edges, using gradient points in model space to control where each color dominates.

Now I'm figuring out how to place the mane cards: building rings of frames around the neck at several points along its chain, each ring generating multiple outward-facing items that cards can be scattered onto with a lean and outward flow direction.

I want the mane to extend onto the head too, but a ring around the head's bone axis would wrap mane strands onto the face, which I don't want. I'm thinking through limiting the ring's angle range or orienting it along a different line so the mane stays on the back/top rather than circling the face entirely.

Simplifying this — rings along the neck from t 0.35 to 1, full 360 degrees, radius 0.26, with cards leaning and bending outward, should cover the head's back acceptably without extra complexity. Cards also inherit a bone reference automatically, and color can tint the grey tuft texture using a Paint read at each card's root, so the SVG texture itself can just be drawn in white/grey tapered strands.

For the face, I'll keep it simple: amber sphere eyes with small black pupil spheres, positioned via the head's local frame using mirrored left/right offsets for symmetry, plus a nose, muzzle, scar, and brows layered on using the same local-coordinate approach relative to the head joint.

Modeling the ears as small rounded spheres on top of the head, the jaw as a separate joint for the lower muzzle, and a thin dark capsule scar across one eyebrow for character detail.

For the paws I'm adding pad spheres attached explicitly to the paw joint, and naming out the limb joint chains — shoulder/elbow/paw for front legs, hip/knee/hock/paw for hind legs — making sure each name is unique and matches the number of points the limb generator returns.

I'm looping over both sides with a sign flip to mirror geometry, naming them L and R, then sweeping the leg chains with tapering radii from shoulder down to paw. For the tail I'm tapering its radius down to a point and capping it with a small dark sphere tuft at the tip.

Now I'm setting up the color palette for the lion -- tawny, cream, gold, chocolate, amber, black, and dark -- and defining a chocolate-to-gold gradient for the mane.

I'm working through the skeleton coordinates: neck chain from chest to head, spine path from hips through the torso, and shoulder joint placement so the front legs sit correctly inside the body volume relative to the belly radius.

Now I'm checking the leg length math for front and hind limbs — verifying the shoulder-to-paw and hip-to-foot distances match the segment lengths I'm assigning so the legs reach the ground naturally without stretching or overlapping.

For the head, I'm sizing a slightly flattened skull sphere, picking a tawny base color that gets mostly hidden under the mane cards, and thinking about adding a neck/head ring of mane so coverage looks continuous around the face.

Placing eyes using the model's local left/forward/up offsets, deciding to skip risky part-scale options and instead use geometry.scale directly on the SphereGeometry for the flattened eye shape, then adding small pupil spheres offset slightly forward, and starting on a black nose sphere next.

Placing a brow scar capsule above the eye for detail. Now I'm working out the jaw joint, positioning it below the head with an aim target, then building the lower muzzle capsule attached to the jaw.

For ears, I'm deciding to keep things simple and add small round spheres positioned to the sides and slightly forward of the head, risking they get mostly hidden under the mane. For the mane rings along the neck, I'm figuring out whether the chain's tangent-based point works directly as a frame source for the ring function, concluding it should since the documentation lists it as a valid frame-kind input.

Now I'm planning the mane to flow back around the neck and chest, using multiple rings with varying radii that bulge outward to simulate volume, with cards angled to lean backward along the natural flow direction. I'm also thinking through coloring the body with a cream belly sector against a tawny base, sweeping the color along the spine chain with radius values that taper at the hips and widen at the chest.

For the tail, I'm designing a long catmull-rom spine curving down from the hips to near the floor, with five named joints forming four tapering spans plus a tip, colored tawny with a darker chocolate tuft of cards at the very end. Now I'm starting to work out the leg chains with narrowing radii from hip to foot.

Working out paw pad placement, I'm adding flattened sphere pads at ground level positioned just above the floor under each leg's foot joint, plus tiny toe spheres offset at the front of each paw for detail.

Checking the geometry stays grounded with paw bottoms and tail tip within tolerance, I'm now importing the builder utilities and starting the module metadata for the lion model.

Setting up color palette and building the base skeleton...

Now I'm working out the neck chain, parenting it off the last spine joint and making sure joint positions line up correctly along the path.

Then I'm defining the head joint using a literal position and direction relative to the neck's end, followed by a jaw joint positioned and aimed using local offsets from the head.

Writing body sweep code...

Then for the neck I'm sweeping a tapered radius profile under the mane, and building the head as a scaled sphere positioned slightly forward and up from the head bone. I'm adding a capsule-shaped muzzle and a flattened, broadened sphere for the nose, both offset forward from the head joint using local coordinates.

Now I'm looping over both sides to place amber eyes with dark pupils and rounded ears, mirroring positions using a sign flip on the left offset, then adding a small scar capsule above one eyebrow for character detail.

I'm working out the exact depth placement so the eyes and scar sit correctly embedded in the ellipsoid skull surface rather than floating or sinking too far in—adjusting forward offsets slightly until the geometry math confirms proper placement at the skull boundary.

Now I'm setting up ring positions for the mane along the neck chain, thinking through how each ring sits in the plane perpendicular to the neck's tangent direction. I'm realizing that at the head end, this disk orientation means mane items could wrap around toward the front of the face rather than staying behind it, so I need to reconsider how the ring geometry projects there.

I'm settling on placing mane rings around t values 0.3, 0.55, and 0.8, with larger radius near the head so the strands frame the face like a halo rather than overlapping it, and I'm also considering whether the mane should extend down toward the chest to look more natural like a real lion's mane.

Now I'm setting up the card generation for the mane tufts — choosing size, lean, and bend parameters, then building a gradient that shifts from golden at the face toward darker chocolate at the outer edges, which should give the mane a nice warm-to-dark fade as it moves from the head down toward the chest and neck.

I'm working out the tail structure next: a tapering radius chain for the tail segments, ending in a tuft ring of small cards at the tip, plus a small dark sphere placed at the tail's endpoint frame for a tufted tip look.

Now I'm setting up leg geometry, defining shoulder and paw anchor points per side and building the limb using a single bend direction for one inner joint, then naming the chain segments shoulder, elbow, and paw for each side.

I'm applying a sweep shape to the front leg chain with tawny coloring, then working out the hind leg equivalent with hip, knee, hock, and paw points and corresponding bend directions, making sure each joint name stays unique across front and hind limbs.

For the paw pads, I'm attaching flattened sphere geometries to the tip joints of each leg chain, handling the possibility that the chain's tip joint could be null by guarding with a conditional check.

Adding toe details...

Now I'm considering the chest shag cards but will skip for simplicity, double-checking the leg parenting to the spine, and settling on a standing-rest pose for the lion. I need to verify how `neck.at(t)` behaves when used for the mane rings, since it returns a point with position and tangent rather than a full frame.

Confirming that chain frames support tangent-based orientation, then moving into writing the jaw, muzzle, and ear geometry with capsules and spheres anchored to local joint offsets. Still writing geometry placements...
